claims.text: The target materials are multicomponent high-entropy alloys having both solid and liquid phases near high melting temperatures, including refractory systems with at least five principal elements.
A deep neural network potential can be applied to both solid and liquid states of a compositionally complex high-entropy material.
The DNN potential should be trained on a wide sampling of ab initio liquid configurations.
The liquid-trained DNN should replace conventional EAM potentials as the thermodynamic-integration reference.
The proposed method applies to refractory high-entropy alloys with melting temperatures exceeding approximately 3000 K.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9–1.0 Tm.
Thermal excitation near melting produces a broad spectrum of liquid atomic configurations.
A DNN potential can represent local environments and liquid-state structural variation in a high-entropy material.
The DNN captures a broader ensemble of atomic configurations and many-body interactions than an EAM reference.
Training on ab initio liquid data allows the DNN to learn complex many-body interactions missing from conventional EAM models.
The broader representation of liquid configurations increases reference–target phase-space overlap.
Increased phase-space overlap reduces mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
The DNN reference will reduce free-energy integration path mismatch by approximately 20–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The reduced integration mismatch will produce more accurate free-energy predictions for high-entropy alloys near melting.
TOR-TILD EAM references struggle to represent the full diversity of configurations in the ab initio liquid.
The benefit should be greatest for compositionally complex alloys near melting and smaller for simpler or less-disordered alloys.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction may depend on alloy composition and temperature.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing EAM-reference and DNN-reference thermodynamic integration against direct ab initio free-energy benchmarks for the same high-entropy alloy systems.
A reduction of less than 20% in integration mismatch, or failure to converge better toward the ab initio free-energy benchmark, would falsify the hypothesis.
